subject: SQL
title: SELECT
summary: `SELECT` is how you read data out of a table.
notes:
## Source data — Pattern 1: Basic Data Retrieval

All queries run against the shared `employees` table (see `schema.sql`).

![SELECT — source table 1](/study-notes/sql/select/fig-1.png)

---

`SELECT` is how you read data out of a table. `SELECT *` means "every column" — quick for exploring a table, but in real applications it's usually better to name columns explicitly (see topic 2) so the query doesn't break or slow down when the table gains new columns.

## Problem

Display all employee details.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM employees;
```

![SELECT — result 2](/study-notes/sql/select/fig-2.png)

subject: SQL
title: SELECT Specific Columns
summary: Listing columns by name instead of `*` returns only what you need — less data moved over the network, and a query that keeps working even if unrelated columns are added to the table later.
notes:
Listing columns by name instead of `*` returns only what you need — less data moved over the network, and a query that keeps working even if unrelated columns are added to the table later.

## Problem

Display employee name and salary.

```sql
SELECT first_name, last_name, salary
FROM employees;
```

![SELECT Specific Columns — result 1](/study-notes/sql/select-specific-columns/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: DISTINCT
summary: `DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows from the result — it looks at the full row (or the listed columns) and collapses repeats down to one.
notes:
`DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows from the result — it looks at the full row (or the listed columns) and collapses repeats down to one. It runs after the columns are selected, so `SELECT DISTINCT department_id` only cares about duplicate `department_id` values, not the whole row.

## Problem

Find all unique departments.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT department_id
FROM employees;
```

![DISTINCT — result 1](/study-notes/sql/distinct/fig-1.png)

## Tip

To show department names instead of IDs, this pairs naturally with a JOIN to `departments` — worth cross-linking once Pattern 6 is live.

subject: SQL
title: Aliases (AS)
summary: `AS` renames a column (or table) in the output only — it doesn't touch the underlying schema.
notes:
`AS` renames a column (or table) in the output only — it doesn't touch the underlying schema. Useful for friendlier report headings, or for naming a computed expression so you can refer to it clearly.

## Problem

Display employee names with the heading 'Employee Name'.

```sql
SELECT first_name AS "Employee Name"
FROM employees;
```

![Aliases (AS) — result 1](/study-notes/sql/aliases-as/fig-1.png)

## Dialect note

MySQL/PostgreSQL accept double quotes or backticks for the alias; SQL Server uses square brackets (`[Employee Name]`).

subject: SQL
title: Arithmetic Expressions
summary: You can compute new values directly in the `SELECT` list — `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` all work on numeric columns just like a calculator.
notes:
You can compute new values directly in the `SELECT` list — `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` all work on numeric columns just like a calculator. The result is a new, unnamed column unless you alias it (see topic 4).

## Problem

Display salary after adding a ₹5,000 bonus.

```sql
SELECT first_name,
       salary,
       salary + 5000 AS salary_with_bonus
FROM employees;
```

![Arithmetic Expressions — result 1](/study-notes/sql/arithmetic-expressions/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: LIMIT / TOP / FETCH FIRST
summary: These cap how many rows come back, which matters once a table has thousands (or millions) of rows and you only need a preview.
notes:
These cap how many rows come back, which matters once a table has thousands (or millions) of rows and you only need a preview. Every major database does this slightly differently — one of the few places dialect really matters for something this basic.

## Problem

Display the first 5 employees.

```sql
-- MySQL / PostgreSQL / SQLite
SELECT *
FROM employees
LIMIT 5;

-- SQL Server
SELECT TOP 5 *
FROM employees;

-- Oracle
SELECT *
FROM employees
FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;
```

![LIMIT / TOP / FETCH FIRST — result 1](/study-notes/sql/limit-top-fetch-first/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: ORDER BY
summary: Without `ORDER BY`, a database can return rows in any order it finds convenient — nothing guarantees insertion order.
notes:
Without `ORDER BY`, a database can return rows in any order it finds convenient — nothing guarantees insertion order. `ORDER BY column DESC` (or `ASC`, the default) is the only reliable way to control row order in the result.

## Problem

Display employees sorted by salary in descending order.

```sql
SELECT first_name, last_name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC;
```

![ORDER BY — result 1](/study-notes/sql/order-by/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: WHERE
summary: `WHERE` filters rows before grouping or sorting happens — it runs on raw table rows, one at a time, and only lets through the ones that match the condition.
notes:
## Source data — Pattern 2: Filtering Data

All queries run against the shared `employees` table (see `schema.sql`). This pattern also needs the `manager_id` column for topic 14 — not required back in Pattern 1. It also needs one row with `salary < 50000` for topic 9, which Pattern 1's 6 rows didn't have — add:

```sql
INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, first_name, last_name, salary, department_id,
manager_id)
VALUES (7, 'Zoya', 'Khan', 42000, 500, 1);
```

![WHERE — source table 1](/study-notes/sql/where/fig-1.png)

---

`WHERE` filters rows before grouping or sorting happens — it runs on raw table rows, one at a time, and only lets through the ones that match the condition. It's the single most-used clause after `SELECT`/`FROM`.

## Problem

Find employees earning more than ₹60,000.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 60000;
```

![WHERE — result 2](/study-notes/sql/where/fig-2.png)

subject: SQL
title: Comparison Operators
summary: `WHERE` conditions are built from comparison operators: `=`, `!=` / `<>`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`.
notes:
`WHERE` conditions are built from comparison operators: `=`, `!=` / `<>`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`. These compare a column to a value (or another column) and return true/false per row.

## Problem

Find employees whose salary is less than ₹50,000.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE salary < 50000;
```

![Comparison Operators — result 1](/study-notes/sql/comparison-operators/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: Logical Operators (AND, OR, NOT)
summary: `AND` requires every condition to be true, `OR` requires at least one, and `NOT` inverts a condition.
notes:
`AND` requires every condition to be true, `OR` requires at least one, and `NOT` inverts a condition. Combining them lets one `WHERE` clause express a rule with multiple parts — just watch operator precedence (`AND` binds tighter than `OR`; use parentheses when mixing them).

## Problem

Find IT employees earning more than ₹70,000.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 100    -- 100 = IT
  AND salary > 70000;
```

![Logical Operators (AND, OR, NOT) — result 1](/study-notes/sql/logical-operators-and-or-not/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: BETWEEN
summary: `BETWEEN a AND b` is shorthand for `column >= a AND column <= b` — both ends are inclusive.
notes:
`BETWEEN a AND b` is shorthand for `column >= a AND column <= b` — both ends are inclusive. Reads cleaner than writing the two comparisons out by hand.

## Problem

Find employees with salaries between ₹50,000 and ₹80,000.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 80000;
```

![BETWEEN — result 1](/study-notes/sql/between/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: IN
summary: `IN (list)` is shorthand for a chain of `OR column = value` checks against a fixed list — much easier to read (and write) than several `OR`s once the list grows past two or three values.
notes:
`IN (list)` is shorthand for a chain of `OR column = value` checks against a fixed list — much easier to read (and write) than several `OR`s once the list grows past two or three values.

## Problem

Find employees working in IT or HR.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE department_id IN (100, 200);   -- 100 = IT, 200 = HR
```

![IN — result 1](/study-notes/sql/in/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: LIKE
summary: `LIKE` does pattern matching on text using two wildcards: `%` (zero or more characters) and `_` (exactly one character).
notes:
`LIKE` does pattern matching on text using two wildcards: `%` (zero or more characters) and `_` (exactly one character). `'A%'` means "starts with A"; `'%a'` would mean "ends with a".

## Problem

Find employees whose names start with 'A'.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE first_name LIKE 'A%';
```

![LIKE — result 1](/study-notes/sql/like/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
summary: `NULL` means "unknown/absent," not zero or empty string — so `= NULL` never matches anything and always silently returns no rows.
notes:
`NULL` means "unknown/absent," not zero or empty string — so `= NULL` never matches anything and always silently returns no rows. Checking for missing values needs the dedicated `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` operators instead.

## Problem

Find employees who do not have a manager assigned.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE manager_id IS NULL;
```

![IS NULL / IS NOT NULL — result 1](/study-notes/sql/is-null-is-not-null/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: String Functions
summary: String functions transform text values — `UPPER()`/`LOWER()` change case, `TRIM()` strips whitespace, `SUBSTRING()` pulls out part of a string.
notes:
## Source data — Pattern 3: Built-in Functions

All queries run against the shared `employees` table (see `schema.sql`). This pattern needs two columns not used before: `hire_date` (topic 17) and `bonus`, nullable (topics 19–20).

![String Functions — source table 1](/study-notes/sql/string-functions/fig-1.png)

---

String functions transform text values — `UPPER()`/`LOWER()` change case, `TRIM()` strips whitespace, `SUBSTRING()` pulls out part of a string. They're applied per-row in the `SELECT` list and don't change the stored data, only the output.

## Problem

Convert all employee names to uppercase.

```sql
SELECT UPPER(first_name) AS first_name_upper,
       UPPER(last_name)  AS last_name_upper
FROM employees;
```

![String Functions — result 2](/study-notes/sql/string-functions/fig-2.png)

subject: SQL
title: Numeric Functions
summary: Numeric functions do math on numbers — `ROUND()`, `CEIL()`/`FLOOR()`, `ABS()`, `POWER()`.
notes:
Numeric functions do math on numbers — `ROUND()`, `CEIL()`/`FLOOR()`, `ABS()`, `POWER()`. `ROUND(value, -3)` rounds to the nearest thousand: a negative second argument rounds to the left of the decimal point instead of the right.

## Problem

Round salaries to the nearest thousand.

```sql
SELECT first_name,
       salary,
       ROUND(salary, -3) AS salary_rounded
FROM employees;
```

![Numeric Functions — result 1](/study-notes/sql/numeric-functions/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: Date Functions
summary: Date functions extract or manipulate parts of a date — `YEAR()`, `MONTH()`, `DATEDIFF()`, `CURRENT_DATE`.
notes:
Date functions extract or manipulate parts of a date — `YEAR()`, `MONTH()`, `DATEDIFF()`, `CURRENT_DATE`. "This year" isn't a fixed value, so the query needs to compare against whatever the database considers today, not a hardcoded year.

## Problem

Find employees hired this year.

```sql
-- MySQL
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE YEAR(hire_date) = YEAR(CURDATE());

-- PostgreSQL / Oracle / standard SQL
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date) = EXTRACT(YEAR FROM CURRENT_DATE);
```

![Date Functions — result 1](/study-notes/sql/date-functions/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: CASE WHEN
summary: `CASE WHEN ...
notes:
`CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END` is SQL's if/else — it evaluates conditions top to bottom and returns the result tied to the first one that matches, falling through to `ELSE` if none do. It's an expression, so it can sit anywhere a column would.

## Problem

Categorize salaries as High, Medium, or Low.

```sql
SELECT first_name,
       salary,
       CASE
         WHEN salary >= 100000 THEN 'High'
         WHEN salary >= 60000  THEN 'Medium'
         ELSE 'Low'
       END AS salary_band
FROM employees;
```

![CASE WHEN — result 1](/study-notes/sql/case-when/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: COALESCE
summary: `COALESCE(a, b, c, ...)` returns the first argument that isn't `NULL`.
notes:
`COALESCE(a, b, c, ...)` returns the first argument that isn't `NULL`. With two arguments it reads as "use this value, but fall back to that default if it's missing" — the most common real-world use is exactly this: replacing `NULL` with a sensible default.

## Problem

Replace NULL bonus values with 0.

```sql
SELECT employee_id,
       bonus,
       COALESCE(bonus, 0) AS bonus_or_zero
FROM employees;
```

![COALESCE — result 1](/study-notes/sql/coalesce/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: NULLIF
summary: `NULLIF(a, b)` returns `NULL` if `a` equals `b`, otherwise returns `a`.
notes:
`NULLIF(a, b)` returns `NULL` if `a` equals `b`, otherwise returns `a`. It's the reverse of COALESCE, and its classic use is guarding a division: dividing by an actual `0` errors or returns infinity depending on the engine, but dividing by `NULLIF(x, 0)` turns that `0` into `NULL` first, so the division safely returns `NULL` instead.

## Problem

Avoid division by zero using NULLIF.

```sql
SELECT employee_id,
       salary,
       bonus,
       salary / NULLIF(bonus, 0) AS salary_to_bonus_ratio
FROM employees;
```

![NULLIF — result 1](/study-notes/sql/nullif/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: CONCAT
summary: `CONCAT()` joins strings together.
notes:
`CONCAT()` joins strings together. Most databases also support the `||` operator as shorthand (SQL Server uses `+` instead) — `CONCAT()` is the more portable choice since it works the same way almost everywhere.

## Problem

Display full name by combining first and last names.

```sql
SELECT CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) AS full_name
FROM employees;
```

![CONCAT — result 1](/study-notes/sql/concat/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: LENGTH / CHAR_LENGTH
summary: `LENGTH()` (MySQL/PostgreSQL/Oracle) or `LEN()` (SQL Server) returns how many characters are in a string — useful for validation rules or, here, filtering rows by name length.
notes:
`LENGTH()` (MySQL/PostgreSQL/Oracle) or `LEN()` (SQL Server) returns how many characters are in a string — useful for validation rules or, here, filtering rows by name length. `CHAR_LENGTH()` is the standard-SQL alias that's explicit about counting characters rather than bytes.

## Problem

Find employees whose names contain more than 8 characters.

```sql
SELECT first_name,
       last_name,
       LENGTH(CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)) AS name_length
FROM employees
WHERE LENGTH(CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)) > 8;
```

![LENGTH / CHAR_LENGTH — result 1](/study-notes/sql/length-char-length/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: COUNT
summary: `COUNT(*)` counts rows, including ones with `NULL`s in every column.
notes:
## Source data — Pattern 4: Aggregation

All queries run against the shared `employees` table (see `schema.sql`) — no new columns needed for this pattern.

![COUNT — source table 1](/study-notes/sql/count/fig-1.png)

---

`COUNT(*)` counts rows, including ones with `NULL`s in every column. `COUNT(column_name)` counts only the rows where that specific column isn't `NULL` — the two can give different answers on the same table, so pick deliberately.

## Problem

Count total employees.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_employees
FROM employees;
```

![COUNT — result 2](/study-notes/sql/count/fig-2.png)

subject: SQL
title: SUM
summary: `SUM()` adds up a numeric column across all matching rows, collapsing them into a single value.
notes:
`SUM()` adds up a numeric column across all matching rows, collapsing them into a single value. Rows with `NULL` in that column are silently skipped, not treated as zero.

## Problem

Find the total salary paid.

```sql
SELECT SUM(salary) AS total_salary
FROM employees;
```

![SUM — result 1](/study-notes/sql/sum/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: AVG
summary: `AVG()` is the mean — sum divided by count — computed only over the non-`NULL` values in that column.
notes:
`AVG()` is the mean — sum divided by count — computed only over the non-`NULL` values in that column. Like `SUM()`, `NULL`s are excluded rather than counted as zero, which can quietly change the result if a column has gaps.

## Problem

Find the average salary.

```sql
SELECT AVG(salary) AS average_salary
FROM employees;
```

![AVG — result 1](/study-notes/sql/avg/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: MIN / MAX
summary: `MIN()` and `MAX()` return the smallest and largest value in a column.
notes:
`MIN()` and `MAX()` return the smallest and largest value in a column. They work on numbers, dates, and even text (alphabetical order) — and like the other aggregates, they collapse the whole result set into one row unless paired with `GROUP BY` (Pattern 5).

## Problem

Find the highest and lowest salary.

```sql
SELECT MAX(salary) AS highest_salary,
       MIN(salary) AS lowest_salary
FROM employees;
```

![MIN / MAX — result 1](/study-notes/sql/min-max/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: Aggregate on Condition
summary: Aggregate functions can follow a `WHERE` clause just like any other query — the filter narrows down which rows get aggregated, so the calculation only runs over the subset that matches.
notes:
Aggregate functions can follow a `WHERE` clause just like any other query — the filter narrows down which rows get aggregated, so the calculation only runs over the subset that matches.

## Problem

Find the total salary of IT employees.

```sql
SELECT SUM(salary) AS it_total_salary
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 100;   -- 100 = IT
```

![Aggregate on Condition — result 1](/study-notes/sql/aggregate-on-condition/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: GROUP BY
summary: `GROUP BY` collapses rows that share a value into one row per group, and any aggregate function in the `SELECT` list (`SUM`, `AVG`, `COUNT`...) then runs per group instead of over the whole table.
notes:
## Source data — Pattern 5: Grouping

All queries run against the shared `employees` table (see `schema.sql`). This pattern needs two new columns — `city` (topic 30) and `job_role` (topic 31) — and enough rows in one department to actually cross a "more than 5" threshold (topic 29), so IT grows from 2 employees to 7.

![GROUP BY — source table 1](/study-notes/sql/group-by/fig-1.png)

---

`GROUP BY` collapses rows that share a value into one row per group, and any aggregate function in the `SELECT` list (`SUM`, `AVG`, `COUNT`...) then runs per group instead of over the whole table.

## Problem

Find total salary by department.

```sql
SELECT department_id,
       SUM(salary) AS total_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id;
```

![GROUP BY — result 2](/study-notes/sql/group-by/fig-2.png)

subject: SQL
title: HAVING
summary: `WHERE` filters individual rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters the groups themselves after aggregation.
notes:
`WHERE` filters individual rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters the groups themselves after aggregation. That's why `HAVING` can reference `COUNT(*)` or `SUM(...)` directly, while `WHERE` can't — the aggregate doesn't exist yet at the point `WHERE` runs.

## Problem

Find departments having more than 5 employees.

```sql
SELECT department_id,
       COUNT(*) AS employee_count
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
```

![HAVING — result 1](/study-notes/sql/having/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: GROUP BY Multiple Columns
summary: Grouping by more than one column creates one group per unique combination of those columns, not one group per column.
notes:
Grouping by more than one column creates one group per unique combination of those columns, not one group per column. Two employees in the same department but different cities land in different groups — grouping by department alone would have merged them.

## Problem

Find average salary by department and city.

```sql
SELECT department_id,
       city,
       AVG(salary) AS average_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id, city;
```

![GROUP BY Multiple Columns — result 1](/study-notes/sql/group-by-multiple-columns/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: COUNT DISTINCT
summary: `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` counts unique values of that column within each group, rather than counting every row.
notes:
`COUNT(DISTINCT column)` counts unique values of that column within each group, rather than counting every row. A department can have several employees but only one or two distinct job roles among them — this is how you'd tell the difference.

## Problem

Find unique job roles in each department.

```sql
SELECT department_id,
       COUNT(DISTINCT job_role) AS unique_roles
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id;
```

![COUNT DISTINCT — result 1](/study-notes/sql/count-distinct/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: INNER JOIN
summary: INNER JOIN returns only the rows where a matching value exists in both tables based on the join condition.
notes:
## Source data — Pattern 6: Joins

All queries run against the shared employees and departments tables (see schema.sql). This pattern introduces the departments table. Topic 38 also needs a projects table, while topic 39 introduces a salary_grades table for non-equi joins.

![INNER JOIN — source table 1](/study-notes/sql/inner-join/fig-1.png)

![INNER JOIN — source table 2](/study-notes/sql/inner-join/fig-2.png)

![INNER JOIN — source table 3](/study-notes/sql/inner-join/fig-3.png)

![INNER JOIN — source table 4](/study-notes/sql/inner-join/fig-4.png)

---

INNER JOIN returns only the rows where a matching value exists in both tables based on the join condition. Rows without a match are excluded from the result.

## Problem

Display employee names with department names.

```sql
SELECT e.first_name,
d.department_name
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
```

![INNER JOIN — result 5](/study-notes/sql/inner-join/fig-5.png)

subject: SQL
title: LEFT JOIN
summary: LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right table.
notes:
LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right table. If no match exists, the right-side columns return NULL.

## Problem

Display all employees, including those without a department.

```sql
SELECT e.first_name,
d.department_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
```

![LEFT JOIN — result 1](/study-notes/sql/left-join/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: RIGHT JOIN
summary: RIGHT JOIN returns all rows from the right table and matching rows from the left table.
notes:
RIGHT JOIN returns all rows from the right table and matching rows from the left table. If no employee belongs to a department, employee columns return NULL.

## Problem

Display all departments, including those without employees.

```sql
SELECT e.first_name,
d.department_name
FROM employees e
RIGHT JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
```

![RIGHT JOIN — result 1](/study-notes/sql/right-join/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: FULL OUTER JOIN
summary: FULL OUTER JOIN returns every row from both tables.
notes:
FULL OUTER JOIN returns every row from both tables. Matching rows are combined, while non-matching rows contain NULL values.

## Problem

Display all employees and departments.

```sql
SELECT e.first_name,
d.department_name
FROM employees e
FULL OUTER JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id;
```

![FULL OUTER JOIN — result 1](/study-notes/sql/full-outer-join/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: CROSS JOIN
summary: CROSS JOIN returns every possible combination of rows from both tables without a join condition.
notes:
CROSS JOIN returns every possible combination of rows from both tables without a join condition.

## Problem

Generate all employee-department combinations.

```sql
SELECT e.first_name,
d.department_name
FROM employees e
CROSS JOIN departments d;
```

![CROSS JOIN — result 1](/study-notes/sql/cross-join/fig-1.png)

## Note

Only the first 12 rows are shown. The complete CROSS JOIN result contains 36 rows (6 employees × 6 departments).

subject: SQL
title: SELF JOIN
summary: A SELF JOIN joins a table to itself using different aliases.
notes:
A SELF JOIN joins a table to itself using different aliases. It is commonly used to relate employees to their managers.

## Problem

Find employees and their managers.

```sql
SELECT e.first_name AS employee,
m.first_name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m
ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;
```

![SELF JOIN — result 1](/study-notes/sql/self-join/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: Multiple JOINs
summary: Multiple JOINs combine data from more than two related tables in a single query.
notes:
Multiple JOINs combine data from more than two related tables in a single query.

## Problem

Display employee, department, and project names.

```sql
SELECT e.first_name,
d.department_name,
p.project_name
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN departments d
ON e.department_id = d.department_id
INNER JOIN projects p
ON e.project_id = p.project_id;
```

![Multiple JOINs — result 1](/study-notes/sql/multiple-joins/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: Non-Equi Join
summary: A non-equi join uses comparison operators such as BETWEEN, < or > instead of equality.
notes:
A non-equi join uses comparison operators such as BETWEEN, < or > instead of equality.

## Problem

Find salary grades using salary ranges.

```sql
SELECT e.first_name,
s.grade
FROM employees e
JOIN salary_grades s
ON e.salary BETWEEN s.min_salary AND s.max_salary;
```

![Non-Equi Join — result 1](/study-notes/sql/non-equi-join/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: UNION
summary: UNION combines the results of two or more SELECT statements into a single result set while removing duplicate rows.
notes:
## Source data — Pattern 7: Set Operators

All queries run against the shared employees table (see `schema.sql`). This pattern introduces the `former_employees` table. Topic 44 also introduces a `retired_employees` table to demonstrate combining multiple set operators in a single query.

![UNION — source table 1](/study-notes/sql/union/fig-1.png)

![UNION — source table 2](/study-notes/sql/union/fig-2.png)

![UNION — source table 3](/study-notes/sql/union/fig-3.png)

---

UNION combines the results of two or more SELECT statements into a single result set while removing duplicate rows. Each SELECT statement must return the same number of columns in the same order with compatible data types.

## Problem

Display the names of all current and former employees without duplicates.

```sql
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM employees
UNION
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM former_employees;
```

![UNION — result 4](/study-notes/sql/union/fig-4.png)

subject: SQL
title: UNION ALL
summary: UNION ALL combines multiple result sets but keeps duplicate rows.
notes:
UNION ALL combines multiple result sets but keeps duplicate rows. Since duplicate removal is not performed, it is generally faster than UNION.

## Problem

Display the names of all current and former employees, including duplicate records.

```sql
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM employees
UNION ALL
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM former_employees;
```

![UNION ALL — result 1](/study-notes/sql/union-all/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: INTERSECT
summary: INTERSECT returns only the rows that exist in both result sets.
notes:
INTERSECT returns only the rows that exist in both result sets. Both queries must have the same number of columns with compatible data types.

## Problem

Find employees who appear in both the current employees and former employees tables.

```sql
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM employees
INTERSECT
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM former_employees;
```

![INTERSECT — result 1](/study-notes/sql/intersect/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: EXCEPT / MINUS
summary: EXCEPT returns rows from the first query that do not appear in the second query.
notes:
EXCEPT returns rows from the first query that do not appear in the second query. Oracle uses MINUS instead of EXCEPT.

## Problem

Display employees who are currently working but are not present in the former employees table. -- SQL Server / PostgreSQL

```sql
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM employees
EXCEPT
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM former_employees;

-- Oracle
```

```sql
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM employees
MINUS
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM former_employees;
```

subject: SQL
title: Scalar Subquery
summary: A scalar subquery returns exactly one value.
notes:
## Source data — Pattern 8: Subqueries

All queries run against the shared `employees` and `departments` tables (see `schema.sql`). This pattern introduces scalar, correlated, and multiple-row subqueries. Topics 47 and 48 demonstrate the EXISTS and NOT EXISTS operators, while Topics 49 and 50 introduce the ANY (SOME) and ALL comparison operators.

![Scalar Subquery — source table 1](/study-notes/sql/scalar-subquery/fig-1.png)

![Scalar Subquery — source table 2](/study-notes/sql/scalar-subquery/fig-2.png)

---

A scalar subquery returns exactly one value. It can be used anywhere a single value or expression is expected, such as in the SELECT, WHERE, or HAVING clause.

## Problem

Find employees earning more than the average salary.

```sql
SELECT first_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (
SELECT AVG(salary)
FROM employees
);
```

![Scalar Subquery — result 3](/study-notes/sql/scalar-subquery/fig-3.png)

subject: SQL
title: Correlated Subquery
summary: A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query.
notes:
A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query. It executes once for every row processed by the outer query.

## Problem

Find employees earning above their department's average salary.

```sql
SELECT first_name, salary
FROM employees e
WHERE salary > (
SELECT AVG(salary)
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = e.department_id
);
```

![Correlated Subquery — result 1](/study-notes/sql/correlated-subquery/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: IN Subquery
summary: An IN subquery returns multiple values.
notes:
An IN subquery returns multiple values. The outer query checks whether a value matches any value returned by the subquery.

## Problem

Find employees working in departments located in Delhi.

```sql
SELECT first_name
FROM employees
WHERE department_id IN (
SELECT department_id
FROM departments
WHERE location = 'Delhi'
);
```

![IN Subquery — result 1](/study-notes/sql/in-subquery/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: EXISTS
summary: The EXISTS operator returns TRUE if the subquery returns at least one row.
notes:
The EXISTS operator returns TRUE if the subquery returns at least one row.

## Problem

Find departments that have employees.

```sql
SELECT department_name
FROM departments d
WHERE EXISTS (
SELECT 1
FROM employees e
WHERE e.department_id = d.department_id
);
```

![EXISTS — result 1](/study-notes/sql/exists/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: NOT EXISTS
summary: The NOT EXISTS operator returns TRUE only when the subquery returns no rows.
notes:
The NOT EXISTS operator returns TRUE only when the subquery returns no rows.

## Problem

Find departments without employees.

```sql
SELECT department_name
FROM departments d
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
SELECT 1
FROM employees e
WHERE e.department_id = d.department_id
);
```

![NOT EXISTS — result 1](/study-notes/sql/not-exists/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: ANY (SOME)
summary: The ANY (or SOME) operator compares a value with each value returned by the subquery.
notes:
The ANY (or SOME) operator compares a value with each value returned by the subquery. The condition is true if it matches at least one value.

## Problem

Find employees earning more than any HR employee.

```sql
SELECT first_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > ANY (
SELECT salary
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 200
);
```

![ANY (SOME) — result 1](/study-notes/sql/any-some/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: ALL
summary: The ALL operator compares a value with every value returned by the subquery.
notes:
The ALL operator compares a value with every value returned by the subquery. The condition is true only if it satisfies the comparison for all returned values.

## Problem

Find employees earning more than all HR employees.

```sql
SELECT first_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > ALL (
SELECT salary
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 200
);
```

![ALL — result 1](/study-notes/sql/all/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: Nested Subqueries
summary: A nested subquery is a subquery inside another subquery.
notes:
A nested subquery is a subquery inside another subquery. It is commonly used to solve complex problems such as finding the second highest salary.

## Problem

Find the second highest salary using subqueries.

```sql
SELECT MAX(salary)
FROM employees
WHERE salary < (
SELECT MAX(salary)
FROM employees
);
```

![Nested Subqueries — result 1](/study-notes/sql/nested-subqueries/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: Basic CTE
summary: A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a temporary named result set created using the WITH clause.
notes:
## Source data — Pattern 9: Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

All queries run against the shared employees and departments tables (see schema.sql). This pattern introduces Common Table Expressions (CTEs). Topic 54 demonstrates a recursive CTE using the employee-manager hierarchy from the employees table.

![Basic CTE — source table 1](/study-notes/sql/basic-cte/fig-1.png)

![Basic CTE — source table 2](/study-notes/sql/basic-cte/fig-2.png)

---

A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a temporary named result set created using the WITH clause. It improves readability and simplifies complex queries.

## Problem

Display employees earning above average.

```sql
WITH avg_salary AS (
  SELECT AVG(salary) avg_sal FROM employees
)
SELECT first_name,salary
FROM employees,avg_salary
WHERE salary>avg_sal;
```

![Basic CTE — result 3](/study-notes/sql/basic-cte/fig-3.png)

subject: SQL
title: Multiple CTEs
summary: Multiple CTEs can be declared in a single WITH clause and referenced together.
notes:
Multiple CTEs can be declared in a single WITH clause and referenced together.

## Problem

Calculate department salary summaries.

```sql
WITH dept_salary AS (
  SELECT department_id,SUM(salary) total_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department_id
), dept_count AS (
  SELECT department_id,COUNT(*) total_emp FROM employees GROUP BY department_id
)
SELECT * FROM dept_salary JOIN dept_count USING(department_id);
```

![Multiple CTEs — result 1](/study-notes/sql/multiple-ctes/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: Recursive CTE
summary: A recursive CTE repeatedly executes until no new rows are produced.
notes:
A recursive CTE repeatedly executes until no new rows are produced. It is commonly used for hierarchical data.

## Problem

Display employee-manager hierarchy.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE emp_tree AS (
  SELECT employee_id,first_name,manager_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.employee_id,e.first_name,e.manager_id FROM employees e JOIN emp_tree t ON
e.manager_id=t.employee_id
)
SELECT * FROM emp_tree;
```

![Recursive CTE — result 1](/study-notes/sql/recursive-cte/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: ROW_NUMBER()
summary: Assigns a unique row number within a result set.
notes:
## Source data — Pattern 10: Window Functions

All queries run against the shared employees table (see schema.sql). This pattern introduces a sales table to demonstrate window functions including ranking, navigation, running totals, moving averages and window aggregates.

![ROW_NUMBER() — source table 1](/study-notes/sql/row-number/fig-1.png)

![ROW_NUMBER() — source table 2](/study-notes/sql/row-number/fig-2.png)

Assigns a unique row number within a result set.

Assign row numbers to sales.

```sql
SELECT *,
ROW_NUMBER() OVER(ORDER BY sales_amount DESC) AS result
FROM sales;
```

subject: SQL
title: RANK()
summary: Ranks rows with gaps after ties.
notes:
Ranks rows with gaps after ties.

Rank employees by sales.

```sql
SELECT *,
RANK() OVER(ORDER BY sales_amount DESC) AS result
FROM sales;
```

subject: SQL
title: DENSE_RANK()
summary: Ranks rows without gaps after ties.
notes:

Assign dense ranks based on sales.

```sql
SELECT *,
DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY sales_amount DESC) AS result
FROM sales;
```

subject: SQL
title: NTILE()
summary: Divides rows into equal-sized buckets.
notes:
Divides rows into equal-sized buckets.

Divide employees into four salary groups.

```sql
SELECT first_name,salary,
NTILE(4) OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC) AS result
FROM employees;
```

subject: SQL
title: LEAD()
summary: Accesses the next row.
notes:
Accesses the next row.

Display the next month's sales.

```sql
LEAD(sales_amount) OVER(ORDER BY sale_month) AS result
FROM sales;
```

![LEAD() — result 1](/study-notes/sql/lead/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: LAG()
summary: Accesses the previous row.
notes:
Accesses the previous row.

## Problem

Display the previous month's sales.

```sql
SELECT *,
LAG(sales_amount) OVER(ORDER BY sale_month) AS result
FROM sales;
```

![LAG() — result 1](/study-notes/sql/lag/fig-1.png)

subject: SQL
title: FIRST_VALUE()
summary: Returns first value in a window.
notes:
Returns first value in a window.

## Problem

Display the first sale in each department.

```sql
SELECT *,
FIRST_VALUE(sales_amount) OVER(PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY
sale_month) AS result
FROM sales;
```

subject: SQL
title: LAST_VALUE()
summary: Returns last value in a window.
notes:
Returns last value in a window.

## Problem

Display the last sale in each department.

```sql
SELECT *,
LAST_VALUE(sales_amount) OVER(PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY sale_month
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS result
```

subject: SQL
title: Running Total

notes:
Calculates cumulative totals.

Calculate cumulative sales.

```sql
SELECT *,
SUM(sales_amount) OVER(ORDER BY sale_month) AS result
FROM sales;
```

Calculate a 3-month moving average.

```sql
AVG(sales_amount) OVER(ORDER BY sale_month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND
```

notes:
## Source data — Pattern 11: Interview SQL Patterns

All queries run against the shared employees table (see schema.sql). Topics 71 and 72 introduce an orders table to solve consecutive records and gaps-and-islands problems. Topics 73 and 74 introduce a monthly_sales table to demonstrate PIVOT and UNPIVOT operations.

![Second Highest Salary — source table 4](/study-notes/sql/second-highest-salary/fig-4.png)

---

Finds the second largest salary using SQL.

## Problem

Find the second highest salary.

summary: Uses DENSE_RANK() to retrieve the nth highest salary.
notes:
Uses DENSE_RANK() to retrieve the nth highest salary.

## Problem

Find the nth highest salary.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT first_name,salary,DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC) rnk

) t
```

title: Top N Per Group
summary: Uses window functions to return the top records within each group.

```sql
FROM (
  SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) rn
  FROM employees
) t
WHERE rn=1;
```

```sql
MERGE INTO employees e
```

subject: SQL
title: Views

## Source data — Pattern 13: Database Objects

A view is a virtual table created from the result of a SQL query. It simplifies complex queries and improves security by exposing only required data.

Create a view for active employees.

```sql
SELECT *
```

subject: SQL
title: Stored Procedures
summary: A stored procedure is a precompiled collection of SQL statements that can be executed repeatedly with input parameters.
notes:
A stored procedure is a precompiled collection of SQL statements that can be executed repeatedly with input parameters.

## Problem

Create a procedure to fetch employees by department.

```sql
CREATE PROCEDURE GetEmployeesByDepartment
  @DeptId INT
AS
BEGIN
SELECT *
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = @DeptId;
END;
```

notes:
A user-defined function (UDF) accepts input parameters and returns a value or table that can be reused in SQL queries.

## Problem

Create a function to calculate annual salary.

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION CalculateAnnualSalary(@MonthlySalary DECIMAL(10,2))
RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2)
```

subject: SQL
title: Triggers
summary: A trigger is a special type of stored program that automatically executes when INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE operations occur.
notes:
A trigger is a special type of stored program that automatically executes when INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE operations occur.

## Problem

Log salary updates automatically.

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER trg_salary_update
ON employees
AFTER UPDATE
AS
BEGIN
INSERT INTO salary_log(employee_id,old_salary,new_salary)
SELECT d.employee_id,d.salary,i.salary
FROM deleted d
JOIN inserted i
ON d.employee_id=i.employee_id;
END;
```

## Source data — Pattern 14: Database Design & Performance

All queries run against the shared employees table (see schema.sql). This pattern introduces performance optimization and transaction management. Topic 85 introduces an accounts table to demonstrate COMMIT and ROLLBACK using a money transfer transaction.

![Indexes — source table 2](/study-notes/sql/indexes/fig-2.png)

An index improves query performance by allowing the database engine to locate rows more efficiently.

subject: SQL
title: Transactions (COMMIT / ROLLBACK)
summary: A transaction is a sequence of SQL statements executed as a single unit.
notes:
A transaction is a sequence of SQL statements executed as a single unit. COMMIT permanently saves changes, while ROLLBACK undoes them if an error occurs.

## Problem

Transfer salary between accounts using a transaction.

```sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 5000
WHERE account_id = 101;
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 5000
WHERE account_id = 102;
COMMIT;
-- Use ROLLBACK instead of COMMIT if an error occurs.
```

![Transactions (COMMIT / ROLLBACK) — result 1](/study-notes/sql/transactions-commit-rollback/fig-1.png)
